claim: The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans orients to the earth's magnetic field during vertical burrowing migrations.
source: We show that the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans orients to the earth's magnetic field during vertical burrowing migrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral experiments showing directional migration in response to magnetic fields, as described in the Results section and shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: Well-fed C. elegans worms migrated up during vertical burrowing.
source: Well-fed worms migrated up, while starved worms migrated down.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from burrowing assays shown in Figure 2G and Figure 3D.

claim: Starved C. elegans worms migrated down during vertical burrowing.
source: Well-fed worms migrated up, while starved worms migrated down.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from burrowing assays shown in Figure 2G and Figure 3D.

claim: C. elegans populations isolated from around the world migrated at angles to the magnetic vector that would optimize vertical translation in their native soil.
source: Populations isolated from around the world, migrated at angles to the magnetic vector that would optimize vertical translation in their native soil, with northern- and southern-hemisphere worms displaying opposite migratory preferences.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing strains from England, Australia, and Hawaii shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: Northern- and southern-hemisphere C. elegans worms display opposite migratory preferences.
source: Populations isolated from around the world, migrated at angles to the magnetic vector that would optimize vertical translation in their native soil, with northern- and southern-hemisphere worms displaying opposite migratory preferences.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing British (northern hemisphere) and Australian (southern hemisphere) strains shown in Figure 3.

claim: Magnetic orientation and vertical migrations in C. elegans require the TAX-4 cyclic nucleotide-gated ion channel in the AFD sensory neuron pair.
source: Magnetic orientation and vertical migrations required the TAX-4 cyclic nucleotide-gated ion channel in the AFD sensory neuron pair.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic ablation and rescue experiments shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: AFD neurons respond to magnetic fields even without synaptic input.
source: Calcium imaging showed that these neurons respond to magnetic fields even without synaptic input.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging experiments in synaptic mutants (unc-13 and unc-31) shown in Figure 7G,H.

claim: C. elegans may have adapted magnetic orientation to simplify their vertical burrowing migration by reducing the orientation task from three dimensions to one.
source: C. elegans may have adapted magnetic orientation to simplify their vertical burrowing migration by reducing the orientation task from three dimensions to one.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the observed behavior patterns.

claim: Many organisms such as birds, butterflies and turtles use the magnetic field of the earth to navigate across the globe.
source: Many organisms such as birds, butterflies and turtles use the magnetic field of the earth (geomagnetic field) to navigate across the globe (Johnsen and Lohmann, 2005; Guerra et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Many animals migrate horizontally by preferentially using either the horizontal or vertical component of the earth's magnetic field.
source: Many animals migrate horizontally by preferentially using either the horizontal (e.g., salmon, Quinn et al., 1981), or the vertical component of the earth's field (e.g., turtles, Light et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on salmon and turtles.

claim: Magnetotactic bacteria use the geomagnetic field to migrate roughly vertically by following the magnetic dip line.
source: By contrast, magnetotactic bacteria use the geomagnetic field to migrate roughly vertically by following the magnetic dip line (Blakemore, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Blakemore, 1975.

claim: Magnetotactic bacteria reverse their polarity-seeking preference across hemispheres.
source: Across hemispheres, magnetotactic bacteria reverse their polarity-seeking preference, thus conserving the adaptiveness of the response (Blakemore et al., 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Blakemore et al., 1980.

claim: No magnetosensory neurons have been identified in any animal prior to this study.
source: Despite this progress, no magnetosensory neurons have been identified in any animal (Edelman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Edelman et al., 2015.

claim: The standard wild-type C. elegans lab strain (N2) was originally isolated in Bristol, England.
source: We found that when starved, the wild-type lab strain, N2, originally from Bristol, England (Dougherty and Calhoun, 1948) preferentially migrated down in vertically oriented cylinders, but did not show a burrowing preference when cylinders were arranged horizontally (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dougherty and Calhoun, 1948.

claim: Starved N2 strain worms preferentially migrated down in vertically oriented cylinders.
source: We found that when starved, the wild-type lab strain, N2, originally from Bristol, England (Dougherty and Calhoun, 1948) preferentially migrated down in vertically oriented cylinders, but did not show a burrowing preference when cylinders were arranged horizontally (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: N2 strain worms did not show a burrowing preference when cylinders were arranged horizontally.
source: We found that when starved, the wild-type lab strain, N2, originally from Bristol, England (Dougherty and Calhoun, 1948) preferentially migrated down in vertically oriented cylinders, but did not show a burrowing preference when cylinders were arranged horizontally (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Starved N2 strain worms reversed their burrowing behavior and migrated up when the local magnetic field polarity was reversed.
source: Consistent with magnetic stimuli dictating vertical migration we found that starved N2 strain worms reversed their burrowing behavior and migrated up (Figure 1B red bar).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B (red bar).

claim: C. elegans exhibits strong behavioral responses to electric fields.
source: This precaution was necessary because C. elegans and other animals exhibit strong behavioral responses to electric fields (Gabel et al., 2007; Manière et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gabel et al., 2007 and Manière et al., 2011.

claim: Temperature gradients between the assay's start position and finish position were negligible across time in the magnetic coil system.
source: Temperature gradients between the assay's start position (at the center of the plate) and the finish position (at its edge) were negligible across time, and did not vary significantly whether we imposed a magnetic field of one earth strength, or if we cancelled out the earth's field by imposing a field of equal strength but opposite direction (two-way repeated measures ANOVA, N = 5, p = 0.123).
evidence: This claim is supported by temperature measurements and statistical analysis (ANOVA, p = 0.123).

claim: When the magnetic field around C. elegans was cancelled, they migrated randomly.
source: Under this condition animals migrated randomly, distributing evenly around the circumference of the assay plate (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: C. elegans exposed to a homogeneous magnetic field of 0.325 Gauss showed a biased distribution directed approximately 120° to the imposed magnetic vector.
source: Worms assayed this way showed a biased distribution directed ∼120° to the imposed magnetic vector (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: C. elegans exposed to a magnetic field of 0.650 Gauss migrated approximately 132° to the imposed vector.
source: Increasing the field strength to match the earth's maximum field strength (0.650 Gauss) resulted in worms migrating approximately the same direction (132°) to the imposed vector (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Starved C. elegans migrated at 305° relative to the field vector when exposed to a 0.650 Gauss magnetic field.
source: Surprisingly, if worms were allowed to starve for just 30 min, they reversed their migratory distribution by ∼180°, now migrating at 305° relative to the field vector (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: C. elegans does not migrate simply toward magnetic north like magnetotactic bacteria.
source: These results demonstrate that C. elegans does not migrate simply toward magnetic north like magnetotactic bacteria (Frankel et al., 2006); rather, they display a preference to migrate at particular angles relative to magnetic north that depend on feeding state.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data and comparison with magnetotactic bacteria behavior cited from Frankel et al., 2006.

claim: In Bristol, the earth's magnetic vector enters the ground at approximately 66° of inclination.
source: In Bristol, the earth's magnetic vector enters the ground (north pointing down) at approximately 66° of inclination (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is based on geomagnetic data and is illustrated in Figure 2G.

claim: To optimally orient upward in Bristol, a worm would need to migrate 156° to the magnetic field penetrating the earth.
source: Thus, in Bristol, to optimally orient upward, a worm would need to migrate 156° to the magnetic field penetrating the earth (green arc in Figure 2E,G)
evidence: This claim is based on geometric calculation from the magnetic field inclination in Bristol.

claim: To optimally orient downward in Bristol, a worm would need to migrate 336° to the magnetic field.
source: to optimally orient downward, a worm would need to migrate 336° to the magnetic field (brown arc in Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This claim is based on geometric calculation from the magnetic field inclination in Bristol.

claim: The mean heading of fed N2 worms (132°) did not differ significantly from the upward direction for England (156.3°).
source: We found that the mean heading of fed worms (132°, N = 1268 animals) did not differ significantly from the upward direction for England (156.3°).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (V test) of experimental data.

claim: The mean heading of starved N2 worms (304.6°) did not differ significantly from the downward direction for England (336.3°).
source: Likewise, the mean heading of starved worms (304.6°, N = 1079 animals) did not differ significantly from the downward direction for England (336.3°).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (V test) of experimental data.

claim: Well-fed N2 worms preferentially migrated up in vertically arranged agar-filled pipettes.
source: We found that, consistent with this idea, starved worms preferentially migrated down while well-fed worms migrated up (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Soil nematodes feed on bacteria associated with rotting fruit on the soil surface.
source: Soil nematodes feed on bacteria associated with rotting fruit on the soil surface (Félix and Braendle, 2010) and on root rhizobacteria deep in the soil (Horiuchi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Félix and Braendle, 2010 and Horiuchi et al., 2005.

claim: Soil nematodes feed on root rhizobacteria deep in the soil.
source: Soil nematodes feed on bacteria associated with rotting fruit on the soil surface (Félix and Braendle, 2010) and on root rhizobacteria deep in the soil (Horiuchi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Horiuchi et al., 2005.

claim: Vertical migrations in C. elegans could be associated with travel between distinct food sources.
source: Vertical migrations could be associated with travel between these distinct food sources.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from known feeding behaviors.

claim: The magnetic field of the earth in Adelaide, Australia is similar in strength and angle to that in England but differs in having the opposite polarity.
source: We therefore repeated our magnetic coil system and burrowing assays with wild-type C. elegans worms isolated from Adelaide (Australia) where the magnetic field of the earth is similar in strength and angle to that in England but differs in the key respect of having the opposite polarity (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is based on geomagnetic data illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: Australian C. elegans worms migrated to an earth-strength field at 302.5° if fed.
source: Unlike British worms, we found that Australian worms placed in a plate within our magnetic coil system migrated to an earth-strength field at 302.5° if fed, and 117.4° if starved.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic coil system assays.

claim: Australian C. elegans worms migrated to an earth-strength field at 117.4° if starved.
source: Unlike British worms, we found that Australian worms placed in a plate within our magnetic coil system migrated to an earth-strength field at 302.5° if fed, and 117.4° if starved.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic coil system assays.

claim: Australian worms migrated down when well-fed in the burrowing assay conducted in Texas.
source: Paralleling our magnetic coil system results, we found that in our lab (located in Texas, USA) Australian worms migrated down when well-fed, and they migrated up when starved in the burrowing assay (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Australian worms migrated up when starved in the burrowing assay conducted in Texas.
source: Paralleling our magnetic coil system results, we found that in our lab (located in Texas, USA) Australian worms migrated down when well-fed, and they migrated up when starved in the burrowing assay (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Hawaiian C. elegans worms migrated at angles that would optimally orient them up and down when satiated and starved in Hawaii.
source: Identical results were found for Hawaiian worms which migrated at angles that would optimally orient them up and down when satiated and starved in Hawaiian (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data referenced in Supplementary file 1B.

claim: Unlike magnetotactic bacteria which follow magnetic field lines during their migrations, C. elegans worms migrate at angles to the imposed field that would result in optimal vertical translation in their native locations.
source: Overall, these results suggest that unlike magnetotactic bacteria, which follow magnetic field lines during their migrations, worms migrate at angles to the imposed field that would result in optimal vertical translation in their native locations.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing different geographic strains.

claim: When no magnet was present in the magnet assay, C. elegans worms distributed evenly between two goal areas.
source: We found that when no magnet was present, worms distributed evenly between these two goals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the magnet assay.

claim: When a magnet was present in the magnet assay, C. elegans worms preferentially migrated toward it.
source: However, if the magnet was present, worms preferentially migrated toward it (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presence of the magnet in the magnet assay did not introduce an unwanted thermal gradient.
source: To ensure the presence of the magnet did not introduce an unwanted thermal gradient, we recorded the temperature difference between goals in the presence and absence of a magnet and found that the two treatments did not significantly differ from each other (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by temperature measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The ability of different C. elegans populations to orient to an artificial magnetic field was strongly correlated with the inclination of the magnetic field at their native sites.
source: We found that the ability of different worm populations to orient to an artificial magnetic field was strongly correlated with the inclination (Figure 4B,C) and vertical strength (Figure 4D,E) of the magnetic field at their native sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The ability of different C. elegans populations to orient to an artificial magnetic field was strongly correlated with the vertical strength of the magnetic field at their native sites.
source: We found that the ability of different worm populations to orient to an artificial magnetic field was strongly correlated with the inclination (Figure 4B,C) and vertical strength (Figure 4D,E) of the magnetic field at their native sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: The horizontal component of the magnetic field was a poor predictor of C. elegans magnetotactic ability.
source: The horizontal component of the field, however, was a poor predictor of this magnetotactic ability (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The strong correlation between magnetotaxis performance, local field inclination, and vertical strength allowed successful prediction of the magnetotaxis index of a wild-type isolate from California, USA.
source: The strong correlation between magnetotaxis performance, local field inclination, and vertical strength allowed us to successfully predict the magnetotaxis index of an additional wild-type isolate from California, USA (Figure 4 red circle in panels B-E, Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by predictive analysis based on correlation data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Wild-type C. elegans isolates from equatorial locations where the magnitude of the vertical component was close to or below 0.2 Gauss were either unable or barely able to magnetotax.
source: Wild-type isolates from equatorial locations where the magnitude of the vertical component was close (or below) 0.2 Gauss, were either unable or barely able to magnetotax (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data referenced in Supplementary file 1A.

claim: Like many animals, C. elegans can use the magnetic field's polarity and inclination to guide its migrations.
source: We conclude from these results that like many animals (Johnsen and Lohmann, 2005) C. elegans can use the magnetic field's polarity and inclination to guide its migrations.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data and comparison with other animals cited from Johnsen and Lohmann, 2005.

claim: C. elegans mutants with defects in touch-form mechanosensation (mec-10) displayed normal or nearly normal magnetic orientation.
source: Mutants with severe defects in some sensory modalities displayed normal or nearly normal magnetic orientation (Figure 5). These included worms deficient in the touch-form of mechanosensation (mec-10, Arnadottir et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and cited from Arnadottir et al., 2011.

claim: C. elegans mutants with defects in light detection (lite-1) displayed normal or nearly normal magnetic orientation.
source: Mutants with severe defects in some sensory modalities displayed normal or nearly normal magnetic orientation (Figure 5). These included worms deficient in the touch-form of mechanosensation (mec-10, Arnadottir et al., 2011), light detection (lite-1, Edwards et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and cited from Edwards et al., 2008.

claim: C. elegans mutants with defects in taste (che-1) displayed normal or nearly normal magnetic orientation.
source: Mutants with severe defects in some sensory modalities displayed normal or nearly normal magnetic orientation (Figure 5). These included worms deficient in the touch-form of mechanosensation (mec-10, Arnadottir et al., 2011), light detection (lite-1, Edwards et al., 2008), taste (che-1, Uchida et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and cited from Uchida et al., 2003.

claim: C. elegans mutants with defects in oxygen sensation (gcy-33) displayed normal or nearly normal magnetic orientation.
source: Mutants with severe defects in some sensory modalities displayed normal or nearly normal magnetic orientation (Figure 5). These included worms deficient in the touch-form of mechanosensation (mec-10, Arnadottir et al., 2011), light detection (lite-1, Edwards et al., 2008), taste (che-1, Uchida et al., 2003), and oxygen sensation (gcy-33, Zimmer et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and cited from Zimmer et al., 2009.

claim: C. elegans mutants with mutations in ttx-1 were significantly impaired in magnetotaxis.
source: However, we also found mutants that were significantly impaired in magnetotaxis. This group comprised worms with mutations in genes co-expressed in a single sensory neuron pair called AFD, first implicated in thermosensation (Mori, 1999). These included two independent mutant alleles of ttx-1, important for AFD differentiation
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and cited from Mori, 1999.

claim: The triple mutant lacking guanylyl cyclases gcy-23, gcy-8, and gcy-18 was significantly impaired in magnetotaxis.
source: However, we also found mutants that were significantly impaired in magnetotaxis. This group comprised worms with mutations in genes co-expressed in a single sensory neuron pair called AFD, first implicated in thermosensation (Mori, 1999). These included two independent mutant alleles of ttx-1, important for AFD differentiation, and the triple mutant lacking guanylyl cyclases, gcy-23, gcy-8, and gcy-18, which together are critical for AFD function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: C. elegans mutants with mutations in tax-4 failed to perform magnetic orientation.
source: Furthermore, we identified a set of transduction mutants that failed to perform magnetic orientation. These included two independent mutant alleles of each tax-4 and tax-2 genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: C. elegans mutants with mutations in tax-2 failed to perform magnetic orientation.
source: Furthermore, we identified a set of transduction mutants that failed to perform magnetic orientation. These included two independent mutant alleles of each tax-4 and tax-2 genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: TAX-4 and TAX-2 encode subunits of a cGMP-gated ion channel implicated in sensory transduction in many sensory neurons, including AFD.
source: These encode subunits of a cGMP-gated ion channel already implicated in sensory transduction in many sensory neurons, including AFD (Komatsu et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Komatsu et al., 1996.

claim: C. elegans worms lacking the AFD sensory neurons failed to orient to an artificial magnetic field.
source: We found that worms lacking the AFD sensory neurons failed to orient to an artificial magnetic field, while their unaffected sisters oriented normally (Figure 6A, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic ablation experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Worms with genetically ablated AFD neurons could move and orient normally to olfactory stimuli.
source: This could not be explained by non-specific defects, because these worms could move and orient normally to olfactory stimuli (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ablating sensory neuron pairs ASE and AWC had no effect on C. elegans magnetotaxis.
source: Similarly ablating nearby sensory neuron pairs ASE and AWC had no effect on magnetotaxis.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic ablation experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The sensory ending of the AFD neurons consists of dozens of villi arranged anterior-to-posterior imbedded inside glial cells.
source: The sensory ending of the AFD neurons consists of dozens of villi arranged anterior-to-posterior (in an antenna-like formation) imbedded inside glial cells (Perkins et al., 1986; Doroquez et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Perkins et al., 1986 and Doroquez et al., 2014.

claim: C. elegans worms with viable AFD neurons but lacking villi were unable to orient to artificial magnetic fields.
source: Genetic ablation of the glia surrounding these structures, results in worms with viable AFD neurons but lacking villi (Bacaj et al., 2008). These worms were unable to orient to artificial magnetic fields (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic ablation experiments shown in Figure 6A and cited from Bacaj et al., 2008.

claim: The AFD sensory neurons are required for magnetotaxis in C. elegans.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that the AFD sensory neurons are required for magnetotaxis.
evidence: This claim is based on multiple genetic ablation and rescue experiments shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Specific rescue of TAX-4 in AFD neurons was sufficient to partially restore the ability of tax-4(null) mutant worms to orient to an artificial magnetic field.
source: Specific rescue of TAX-4 in AFD neurons was sufficient to partially restore the ability of tax-4(null) mutant worms to orient to an artificial magnetic field (Figure 6B, AFD+ others-).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Rescuing TAX-4 in all tax-4-expressing neurons using its endogenous promoter did not result in increased rescue compared to AFD-specific rescue.
source: To investigate the possibility that TAX-4 may also mediate magnetic orientation through additional neurons we further rescued TAX-4 in all tax-4-expressing neurons by using its endogenous promoter and regulatory elements. However, this did not result in an increased rescue (Figure 6B, AFD+ others+).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Rescuing tax-4 in all tax-4-expressing neurons except AFD failed to restore magnetotactic ability.
source: To test if tax-4 contributed to magnetotaxis through any other neuron asides from AFD, we tested tax-4 mutants where this gene was rescued in all tax-4-expressing neurons except for the AFD neurons (gift from Dr R Baumeister). While rescuing tax-4 in all but AFD neurons resulted in a rescue of the ability of these animals to orient to chemical stimuli (Supplementary file 1A), these animals remained unable to orient to magnetic fields (Figure 6B, AFD- others+).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The cGMP-gated ion channel TAX-4 plays an important role in the AFD sensory neurons for orientation to magnetic fields.
source: These results support the hypothesis that the cGMP-gated ion channel TAX-4 plays an important role in the AFD sensory neurons for orientation to magnetic fields.
evidence: This claim is based on genetic rescue experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: tax-4 mutant worms did not show preferential vertical migration unless the gene was selectively rescued in the AFD neurons.
source: Consistent with our observations in the magnet and in the magnetic coil assays, tax-4 mutant worms did not show preferential vertical migration unless the gene was selectively rescued in the AFD neurons (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by burrowing assay experiments shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Starved British and Australian wild-type isolates lacking the AFD neurons failed to engage in biased vertical migrations.
source: Starved British and Australian wild-type isolates lacking the AFD neurons similarly failed to engage in biased vertical migrations, although their sisters not carrying the transgene (used to kill AFD) remained able to migrate down or up respectively (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic ablation experiments in burrowing assays shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Exposure of mechanically immobilized C. elegans to an 8-s, 65-Gauss rotating magnetic stimulus produced a transient increase in the average brightness of the AFD neurons.
source: After recording baseline activity (Figure 7B), we exposed mechanically immobilized worms to an 8-s, 65-Gauss (100× earth) rotating (2 Hz) magnetic stimulus (see 'Materials and methods' for details). We observed a transient increase in the average brightness of the AFD neurons (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Successive magnetic stimuli consistently produced a reduced response in AFD neurons.
source: Successive stimuli consistently produced a reduced response (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: AFD neurons responded to magnetic stimuli of 10× and 1× earth strength (6.5 and 0.65 Gauss respectively).
source: We observed a similar response when the magnetic stimulus was decreased to 10× and 1× earth stimuli (6.5 and 0.65 Gauss respectively, Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7E,F.

claim: AFD neurons continued to respond to magnetic fields in worms impaired in rapid and dense-core synaptic transmission (unc-13 and unc-31 mutant strains).
source: To help determine if the AFD neurons themselves are magnetosensitive, and not just synaptically downstream from 'real' magnetoreceptive neuron(s), we measured AFD calcium responses in worms impaired in rapid and dense-core synaptic transmission (unc-13 and unc-31 mutant strains, Ahmed et al., 1992; Ann et al., 1997). In the absence of chemical synaptic or neuromodulatory inputs, the AFD neurons continued to respond to magnetic fields (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data in synaptic mutants shown in Figure 7G,H and cited from Ahmed et al., 1992 and Ann et al., 1997.

claim: Magnetic-induced calcium responses in AFD were not observed in a tax-4 mutant background.
source: Magnetic-induced calcium responses in AFD were not observed in a tax-4 mutant background, suggesting that this requires Ca2+ entering the TAX-4 cGMP-gated ion channel (Figure 7I, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data in tax-4 mutants shown in Figure 7I.

claim: Magnetic responses were not observed in the AWC sensory neuron pair.
source: Responses were also not observed in an adjacent sensory neuron pair AWC (Figure 7J and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: The change in AFD brightness in response to magnetic stimuli was significantly greater than control for all test conditions except in the case of tax-4 mutant background.
source: We found that the change in brightness was significantly greater than control for all test conditions except in the case of tax-4 mutant background (Figure 7K).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: The AFD sensory neurons respond to magnetosensory stimuli relevant to geomagnetic orientation.
source: Our imaging results provide physiological evidence that the AFD sensory neurons respond to magnetosensory stimuli relevant to geomagnetic orientation.
evidence: This claim is based on calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: This study provides the first behavioral and physiological evidence for magnetosensory neurons.
source: Here we provide the first behavioral and physiological evidence for magnetosensory neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on the combined behavioral and physiological data presented in the study.

claim: Nematodes use the AFD neurons to orient to earth-strength magnetic fields.
source: Nematodes unexpectedly appear to use the AFD neurons to orient to earth-strength magnetic fields.
evidence: This claim is based on genetic ablation, rescue, and calcium imaging experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: C. elegans guides its vertical migrations using the geomagnetic field and adjusts preference for up or down depending on their satiation state.
source: C. elegans guides its vertical migrations using the geomagnetic field and adjusts preference for up or down depending on their satiation state.
evidence: This claim is based on burrowing experiments shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: Population variability in C. elegans magnetotactic ability correlates with global field properties, with worms from locations where the field is strong and vertical outperforming those where the field is weak and more horizontal.
source: Population variability in magnetotactic ability correlates with global field properties: with worms from locations where the field is strong and vertical outperforming those where the field is weak and more horizontal.
evidence: This claim is based on correlation analysis of wild isolates shown in Figure 4.

claim: The AFD sensory neuron pair is necessary for magnetic orientation and for vertical migrations in C. elegans.
source: The AFD sensory neuron pair is necessary for magnetic orientation and for vertical migrations.
evidence: This claim is based on genetic ablation experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The cGMP-gated ion channel TAX-4 in the AFD neurons is necessary and sufficient for magnetic orientation and vertical migrations in C. elegans.
source: Similarly, a cGMP-gated ion channel in the AFD neurons, TAX-4, is also necessary and sufficient for these behaviors.
evidence: This claim is based on genetic ablation and rescue experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The role of the AFD sensory neurons in magneto-transduction is supported by their ability to respond to magnetic fields even in the absence of synaptic inputs.
source: The role of the AFD sensory neurons in magneto-transduction is supported by their ability to respond to magnetic fields even in the absence of synaptic inputs.
evidence: This claim is based on calcium imaging experiments in synaptic mutants shown in Figure 7G,H.

claim: The magnetosensory AFD neurons also respond to temperature, CO2, and moisture gradients in a satiation-dependent manner.
source: The magnetosensory AFD neurons also respond to temperature (Mori, 1999), CO2 (Bretscher et al., 2008; 2011), and moisture (Russell et al., 2014) gradients in a satiation-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on AFD function.

claim: Temperature, CO2, and moisture parameters vary with depth in the soil.
source: All of these parameters vary with depth in the soil (Jassal et al., 2005) supporting the role of the AFD neurons in vertical burrowing migrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jassal et al., 2005.

claim: C. elegans performs magnetotaxis in darkness.
source: Because C. elegans performs magnetotaxis in darkness (assays were wrapped in 3-layers of foil), it is possible that it detects fields with nano-scale compasses made of biological magnetic material previously described in C. elegans (Cranfield et al., 2004), rather than by a light-dependent mechanism, although this study did not investigate this possibility.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental design and cited from Cranfield et al., 2004.

claim: Biological magnetic material has been previously described in C. elegans.
source: Because C. elegans performs magnetotaxis in darkness (assays were wrapped in 3-layers of foil), it is possible that it detects fields with nano-scale compasses made of biological magnetic material previously described in C. elegans (Cranfield et al., 2004), rather than by a light-dependent mechanism, although this study did not investigate this possibility.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cranfield et al., 2004.

claim: Magnetic particles may be associated with the anterior and posterior-directed microvilli of the AFD neurons.
source: However, based on our behavioral, mutant, transgenic, and physiological analyses we hypothesize magnetic particles, perhaps such as those found in magnetotactic bacteria (Frankel et al., 2006) and previously reported in C. elegans, may (either directly or indirectly) be associated with the anterior and posterior-directed microvilli of the AFD neurons.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from experimental results and comparison with magnetotactic bacteria.

claim: Magnetic stimulation of AFD structures could lead to activation of unspecified guanylyl cyclases (such as GCY-8, GCY-18, or GCY-23), in turn activating the TAX-4 channel and resulting in Na+ and Ca2+ influx and cell depolarization.
source: Magnetic stimulation of these structures could lead to activation of unspecified guanylyl cyclases (such as GCY-8, GCY-18, or GCY-23), in turn activating the TAX-4 channel and resulting in Na+ and Ca2+ influx and cell depolarization.
evidence: This claim is a hypothetical mechanism based on inference from experimental results.

claim: The magnetic field of the earth provides reliable directional and positional information to organisms capable of its detection.
source: The magnetic field of the earth provides reliable directional and positional information to organisms capable of its detection.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Aside from magnetotactic bacteria, magnetic orientation has been largely observed in animals that migrate horizontally.
source: Aside from magnetotactic bacteria, magnetic orientation has been largely observed in animals that migrate horizontally (Johnsen and Lohmann, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Johnsen and Lohmann, 2005.

claim: The finding that vertical migrations by an animal may be guided by magnetic fields opens a new niche for the study of magnetic navigation.
source: Our finding that vertical migrations by an animal may also be guided by this sensory modality opens a new niche for the study of magnetic navigation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Magnetotactic bacteria passively migrate along field lines with south-seeking bacteria swimming down and north-seeking bacteria swimming up in the southern and northern hemispheres respectively.
source: Magnetotactic bacteria passively migrate along field lines: with south-seeking bacteria swimming down, and north-seeking bacteria swimming up in the southern and northern hemispheres respectively (Frankel et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Frankel et al., 2006.

claim: The difference in migration angles and in response amplitude between wild-type C. elegans isolates from around the world suggests that magnetosensation is under considerable selective pressure.
source: The difference in migration angles and in response amplitude between wild-type isolates from around the world suggests that this sensory modality is under considerable selective pressure and will be the subject of future studies.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing geographic strains.

claim: The finding that the direction of vertical migrations could be reversed by an imposed magnetic field strongly suggests that C. elegans relies on the geomagnetic field rather than gravity.
source: Our findings that the direction of vertical migrations could be reversed by an imposed magnetic field and that wild-type populations of worms from opposite hemispheres displayed opposite vertical migration preference strongly suggests that C. elegans relies on the geomagnetic field rather than gravity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: Wild-type populations of C. elegans worms from opposite hemispheres displayed opposite vertical migration preference.
source: Our findings that the direction of vertical migrations could be reversed by an imposed magnetic field and that wild-type populations of worms from opposite hemispheres displayed opposite vertical migration preference strongly suggests that C. elegans relies on the geomagnetic field rather than gravity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Studies on paramecia suggest that the relative density of the organism against its media is instrumental in gravitaxis.
source: Studies on paramecia suggest that the relative density of the organism against its media is instrumental in gravitaxis (Kuroda and Kamiya, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kuroda and Kamiya, 1989.

claim: For nearly buoyant worms imbedded in a soil matrix, the relative density of their surrounding media is highly variable and may preclude reliance on gravitaxis.
source: However, for nearly buoyant worms imbedded in a soil matrix, the relative density of their surrounding media is highly variable and may preclude reliance on gravitaxis.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference about C. elegans ecology.

claim: Many magnetotactic bacteria use a mechanism known as 'polar magneto-aerotaxis' where these cells preferentially migrate up or down in chemically stratified water or sediment columns using a single sensory pathway to integrate magnetotaxis and aerotaxis.
source: Many magnetotactic bacteria use a mechanism known as 'polar magneto-aerotaxis' where these cells preferentially migrate up or down in chemically stratified water or sediment columns using an single sensory pathway to integrate magnetotaxis and aerotaxis (Blakemore et al., 1980; Frankel et al., 1997; Popp et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Blakemore et al., 1980; Frankel et al., 1997; and Popp et al., 2014.

claim: Like C. elegans, polar magneto-aerotactic bacteria from different hemispheres have adapted their polarity preference to match their native environment.
source: Like C. elegans, polar magneto-aerotactic bacteria from different hemispheres have adapted their polarity preference to match their native environment (Blakemore, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Blakemore, 1975 and comparison with C. elegans data.

claim: The role of magnetotaxis in C. elegans may be to increase the efficiency of taxis to other sensory cues by reducing a search problem from three dimensions to one.
source: It appears that the role of magnetotaxis in C. elegans, as in bacteria, may be to increase the efficiency of taxis to other sensory cues by reducing a search problem from three dimensions to one.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from comparison with bacterial magnetotaxis.

claim: Unlike bacteria which migrate along the dip line at an angle relative to the vertical direction, C. elegans appears to align motion at an angle to the magnetic field that would enable a more vertical trajectory in its native environment.
source: Unlike bacteria which migrate along the dip line at an angle relative to the vertical direction, however, C. elegans appears to align motion at an angle to the magnetic field that would enable a more vertical trajectory in its native environment.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing different geographic strains.

claim: The finding that strains from England, Australia and Hawaii each displayed a preferred magnetic orientation preference that matched the geomagnetic field orientation at their source of isolation rather than the experimental site suggests a genetic encoding of magnetic orientation preference.
source: Our finding that the strains from England, Australia and Hawaii each displayed a preferred magnetic orientation preference that matched the geomagnetic field orientation at their source of isolation rather than the one at the experimental site (Texas, USA) suggests a genetic encoding of magnetic orientation preference.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing strains tested in Texas.

claim: Satiation affects the sign of the response to sensory stimuli that the AFD neurons respond to.
source: From previous work (Bretscher et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2014), it is clear that satiation affects the sign of the response to sensory stimuli that the AFD neurons respond to.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bretscher et al., 2008 and Russell et al., 2014.

claim: Rotting fruit on the surface represents an extremely rich, but transient, food supply for C. elegans.
source: Rotting fruit on the surface represents an extremely rich, but transient, food supply.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about C. elegans ecology.

claim: Rhizobacteria represent a low-quality but stable source of food for C. elegans.
source: By contrast, rhizobacteria represent a low-quality but stable source of food.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about C. elegans ecology.

claim: For a starved C. elegans worm on the surface, burrowing down would be adaptive because it leads to rhizobacteria in the plant roots.
source: For a starved worm on the surface, burrowing down would be adaptive because it leads to rhizobacteria in the plant roots.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference about adaptive behavior.

claim: Worms on poor diets have been shown to be more likely to abandon the relative safety of their food patch in an attempt to find a higher quality source.
source: Worms on poor diets have been shown to be more likely to abandon the relative safety of their food patch in an attempt to find a higher quality source (Shtonda and Avery, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shtonda and Avery, 2006.

claim: Many animal species engage in vertical soil migrations.
source: Many animal species (including other nematodes, Prot, 1980) engage in vertical soil migrations (Price and Benham, 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Prot, 1980 and Price and Benham, 1977.

claim: Magnetic orientation may be more widespread than previously believed.
source: Therefore magnetic orientation may be more widespread than previously believed.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the finding that C. elegans uses magnetic orientation.

claim: The small size, genetic tractability, and research amenability of C. elegans make it an optimal model to begin to unlock potentially conserved cellular-molecular mechanisms by which animals detect and orient to the magnetic field of the earth.
source: While the scale and nature of magnetosensation make it challenging to study in large animals with extensive ranges, the small size, genetic tractability, and research amenability of C. elegans make it an optimal model to begin to unlock potentially conserved cellular-molecular mechanisms by which animals detect and orient to the magnetic field of the earth.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about C. elegans as a model organism and inference about future research potential.

claim: All experiments were conducted at The University of Texas at Austin, Texas, USA between 2011 and 2014.
source: All worms were raised and tested at The University of Texas at Austin, Texas, USA (30° 20′ N 97° 45′ W) between 2011 and 2014.
evidence: This is a factual statement about experimental conditions.

claim: The study conducted over 1200 assays involving more than 61,000 worms.
source: We conducted over 1200 assays (>61,000 worms), averaging ∼48 worms per assay.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the scale of the experiments.

claim: All behavioral assays were conducted with experimenter blind to genotype of the worms assayed.
source: All behavioral assays were conducted with experimenter blind to genotype of the worms assayed.
evidence: This is a factual statement about experimental methodology.
